Four of these the app can act on
the target, the stop, the deadline and the quality threshold. The free text it can store but never read. The stop is what actually limits a loss, it turns "how often am I right" into "how much do I make when I'm right versus lose when I'm wrong", which is the number that decides whether the account grows. The deadline handles the third outcome nobody plans for: the thesis was neither right nor wrong, it just never happened, and the money sat there.

What this list is for
Your sell rule fires when a company is already bad. This shows the ones on the way there, a score sliding from 10 to 7 across two quarters is a business deteriorating on your own criteria, often before the price reflects it. The scores were always being calculated; only the latest one used to be kept. This reads the daily log instead, so it starts thin and gets more useful every week you run a refresh.

Dividend income

How this is worked out
Worked out from your holdings automatically, nothing to log. The Dividends accrued figure above is a projection, not income, it accrues day by day from the rates below, so it grows the longer you hold, whether or not a payment ever lands. Finnhub's free tier doesn't expose actual payment dates or amounts, so this is an estimate at each company's current declared rate; it can't see a cut, a raise, or tax withheld.

How you behave, the pattern in your own trading
Why this one analyses you
Everything else in PerceptFolio analyses companies. This analyses you. Anyone can get price history; nobody else has yours. These are the four questions the ledger can answer about your habits. How long you actually hold, whether you sell too early, whether you keep to your own cash rule, and whether you trade more when things get loud.

Layer deep: who a company depends on

Add a Relationship

What's automatic and what isn't
Supplier and customer links have to be entered by hand. That data is assembled by vendors from filings and transcripts and sold at institutional rates, no free API publishes it. The 10-K is where to find it: any customer worth more than 10% of revenue must be disclosed, usually under "Concentration of Credit Risk" or in the risk factors.

The summary describes the relationship, not the company, so it reads correctly from both ends and is copied to the other company's map automatically. Edit it later on either side and the other side follows, unless you've already written something different there.

What's automatic and what isn't
The centre company's profile and the "similar companies" row come from Finnhub and fill in on their own. Suppliers and customers are yours to enter. Institutional holders were deliberately left out: the free source for that is quarterly 13F filings, which are up to four months stale, exclude short positions entirely, and would list Vanguard, BlackRock and State Street at the top of nearly every company you could look up. A list that says the same thing about everything isn't worth the screen space.

The move, in context

Loading
How the ruler works
The VIX is an annualised expectation of volatility. Divide it by the square root of 252 trading days (15.87, near enough 16) and you get the size of a typical day. This says whether today's move is ordinary or unusual for the current level of fear. It says nothing about direction, it's a ruler, not a forecast.

Calendar effects

not used in any verdict

Rates and the economy

context, not a verdict
Loading
Reading the card
Fed funds is the overnight rate the Fed sets, inside its target range; the 3-month bill tracks it. The 2-year is the market's bet on where that rate goes next; the 10- and 30-year price growth and inflation for decades ahead, and the mortgage rate is what the 10-year costs a household. When the 2-year sits above the 10-year (a negative 2s10s) the curve is inverted, which has preceded most US recessions by a year or so and has also sent false alarms. Inflation is the CPI over the past twelve months, realised; the breakeven is the inflation the bond market expects over the next ten. Unemployment is the labour market as of last month. The balance sheet rising is the Fed buying bonds, falling is the Fed letting them run off. None of it feeds a score or a verdict here. It is the weather the businesses you rate are operating in.

Figures with no free feed

Entering your own figure
A Buffett figure entered here overrides the one calculated from FRED. Worth doing. FRED's Wilshire series is a price index rather than a dollar market cap, so the calculated version tracks the right direction but isn't the textbook percentage. A number from a source that computes it properly is more trustworthy.
Read these as long-run expectations, not crash warnings
All three describe what returns over the next ten to fifteen years are likely to look like from today's prices. They have almost no power to time the next twelve months. The Buffett indicator has read "expensive" since roughly 2013 and CAPE has been above 30 since 2017, through years of large gains. Use them to decide how much to put in, not when to get out.

No calls recorded yet. PerceptFolio starts logging every time its verdict on a ticker changes, from the next Refresh onward; it can't grade calls it never wrote down. Come back once you have a few weeks of history.
How marks are captured
Marks are captured live: when a call crosses its 30/90/180/365-day anniversary and the app is open, the price and SPY at that moment are stamped onto the call permanently. Finnhub's free plan has no historical price lookup, so this is the only way to get a true fixed-horizon record, which means the record starts from today and builds forward. If a call's anniversary passes while the app is closed for too long, it is marked unmarkable and dropped rather than graded at the wrong holding period.
No news loaded yet.
News is fetched on demand so it does not spend your Finnhub quota in the background. Press Refresh, or open a ticker from Portfolio. Headlines are shown as context only: this product never turns a headline into a buy or sell verdict, because a model asked to justify a verdict from headlines will always find a reason.

arithmetic, not a verdict

Portfolio risk

Where your risk actually sits
Risk needs at least two holdings.
This panel splits your risk by where it actually sits rather than by position size, which needs at least two positions with enough price history to estimate volatility. Add holdings in Portfolio and refresh once; it fills in on its own.
Sizing counterfactual. Same trades, different size
This is not a backtest, and the difference matters
It does not choose different stocks, trade on different days, or use a single price that was not already recorded here. Every ticker is one you hold, every date is one this app logged a close for, and every entry and exit stays exactly where it happened. The only thing changed is how many dollars sat in each position. A backtest has to invent prices for trades you never made; this invents nothing, which is why it is allowed to exist here and a backtest is not.
Check any stock's risk
Is the return worth the swings?
Professionals call this the Sharpe ratio.
What Sharpe measures here
Return per unit of volatility, from your own daily snapshots. Shown with its confidence interval, because a Sharpe ratio computed on a few months of data carries an error bar usually wider than the number itself, and a point estimate without one is the same false precision as a hit rate without a sample size.
How bad a bad day gets
Professionals call these Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall.

Signals. Rules that emit a position today
Herizen momentum score
Four segments, not four lookbacks
The strategy as described draws lines from one week, two weeks, one month and two months ago to today, but those windows are nested, so the same recent days are counted in all four and a single sharp move pushes every line at once. A +4 built that way is one observation counted four times. This uses non-overlapping segments instead. Two months to one month, one month to two weeks, two weeks to one week, one week to today, so a +4 means four separate stretches each rose, which is a genuinely stronger statement.

Read this before you trust it

What the evidence actually says
The published evidence on price trends splits sharply by horizon. Momentum, winners keep winning. Is documented at roughly three to twelve months. At one week and one month the documented effect is the opposite: short-term reversal, where recent winners give it back. Three of this rule's four windows sit in that reversal band, which means the honest prior on it is somewhere between "no edge" and "negative edge", before costs.

That is why it is wired in as a position cap and nothing else. It can shrink a position the checklist already cleared. It cannot create a buy, block a sell, or change a verdict. A wrong cap costs you upside; a wrong verdict costs you capital, and this rule has not earned the right to cost you capital.

It is also being graded against two alternatives from today, checklist alone, this alone, and the two combined. On the Market tab. In ninety days that argument settles itself with numbers instead of citations.

Investment policy

How much of the whole portfolio a single position is allowed to put at risk. With a stop set; this is the most you lose if it hits. Without one, it sizes by volatility instead. A flat cap treats a quiet utility and a violent semiconductor as the same bet; this doesn't.

Buy / Sell Rules

These numbers are the verdict. Every check the terminal runs counts toward one score, each in proportion to how much it is worth; the full table is in ANALYSIS-AUDIT.md. A company at or above the buy line says BUY, at or under the sell line says SELL, anything between says HOLD. The same answer whether or not you own it.
Why changing a bar splits the record
Changing a buy or sell bar creates a different system. Every call graded before the change was made by one that no longer exists, so you'll be asked what you expect the change to do and what result would prove it wrong. Before you see any data. That's the only defence against searching a small sample until something looks significant.

Rule change log

What the words mean

Every term this terminal uses, in plain English. Nothing here changes a number; it is the same answer in different words.

Where your book is kept

On the server, under your access code, from your first sign-in. This browser keeps a copy so the terminal is fast and works offline; the server copy is the one that survives a lost laptop. Sign in on another device with the same code and your book is there, on two devices: a desk and a pocket.

Sync with your invite code

Stored on the worker under your code, readable by anyone holding it.

Sync is off for this account

How sync behaves
Once connected it syncs automatically, when you open the app, a few seconds after you make changes, and when you close the tab. This is whole-account last-write-wins, not a merge. If you edit on your phone and your laptop without letting them sync in between, the device that saves last overwrites the other. It warns you before clobbering something newer, but the safe habit is to open the app on a device and let it sync before you start editing there.

Shared calls

API keys

Give a key to an assistant, a script or a spreadsheet and it can read this account. Keys are read-only: nothing holding one can change, trade or delete anything.
The record is your calls, their marks and the hash chain. The book adds your holdings, your cost basis and your cash. Give the narrower one unless the wider is needed.

Your broker

Connect an account and the terminal reads your positions and your trades, and fills the book in for you. The connection is read-only: it cannot place, change or cancel an order. Your broker password is never sent to us, and you can disconnect here at any time.
Not connected.
Trades read from a broker are stored as history, the same as a CSV import. The record does not grade them, because they are not calls this terminal made.
